# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

The interpretive thesis of Section&nbsp;[-@sec-hierarchy] (Bell-correlation form is determined by the algebraic order of the source's conservation law) and the constructive thesis of Section&nbsp;[-@sec-spice] (a classical three-phase analog reproduces Tsirelson saturation) yield, in combination, a number of testable predictions and structural implications. This section develops them, then states the limitations of the framework and the open questions that remain.

## Predictions and testable consequences

Three classes of testable consequence follow from the framework as developed.

*Three-party Bell tests with explicit zero-sequence access.* The interpretive thesis identifies the zero-sequence mode as a real physical degree of freedom mediating the apparent nonlocality of two-party CHSH violations. If this identification is correct, then a three-party Bell test in which the zero-sequence mode is *itself measured* should yield correlations consistent with the Mermin three-party inequality [@mermin1990], saturating the quantum bound $|M| \leq 4$ rather than the Bell bound $|M| \leq 2$. Crucially, the zero-sequence contribution to the three-party correlator should be *directly observable* in the present analog: it is the energy on the common-mode rail, and a third measurement station instrumented to capture that rail should produce a measurement record that, when correlated with Alice and Bob's records, reproduces the Mermin saturation. The relevant experiment is conceptually identical to standard three-party Bell tests but explicitly identifies the third party as the common-mode channel rather than treating it as a third spatial location of a second entangled pair.

*Classical three-phase laboratory tests.* Three-phase power-systems laboratories already possess the apparatus to test the framework directly. The required experiment is: prepare a balanced three-phase source carrying equal positive and negative sequences with controllable amplitudes; measure simultaneously at two independently chosen Park angles; compute the joint correlator $E(\phi_A, \phi_B)$ over many trials with random (uniform) source emission phase $\theta$. The continuous-valued correlator should reproduce $-\tfrac{1}{2}\cos(2\Delta\phi)$ exactly (Section&nbsp;[-@sec-two-party]). Binarization by sign-thresholding should reproduce the deterministic-threshold piecewise-linear correlator with $|S| = 2$. Binarization by random local sampling with probability $\cos^2(\theta - \phi)$ should reproduce the stochastic-local correlator $-\tfrac{1}{2}\cos(2\Delta\phi)$ with $|S| = \sqrt{2}$. Strict event-by-event complementarity, enforced by an active common-mode constraint that makes Alice's and Bob's complementary outcomes coupled trial-by-trial, should reproduce the full Tsirelson-saturating $-\cos(2\Delta\phi)$ with $|S| = 2\sqrt{2}$. The four predictions are testable on standard equipment and would, if confirmed, close the gap between the algebraic claim of Section&nbsp;[-@sec-hierarchy] and direct laboratory observation.

*Higher-symmetry violations.* The three-phase system has the cyclic group $C_3$ as its rotational symmetry. A system with the dihedral group $D_4$ (the symmetry of the square) would possess additional independent quadratic invariants beyond the active power $P$, the reactive power $Q$, and the apparent power $S^2 = P^2 + Q^2$ that the three-phase system supports. Each additional invariant, by the argument of Section&nbsp;[-@sec-hierarchy], should produce its own cos-squared correlator structure, and tests of generalized Bell inequalities involving multiple measurement settings or multiple parties should be able to access these additional invariants. The prediction is that *the size of generalized Bell violations grows with the number of independent quadratic invariants of the source's symmetry group*, and specifically that systems with $D_4$ symmetry should permit larger violations than systems with $C_3$ symmetry on appropriately designed tests.

## Limitations

The framework as developed has several explicit limitations, which are best stated in the user-facing voice of the codebase's own discussion notes. Quoted in our own terms:

The construction does *not* derive the Born rule from first principles. It composes two layers --- the squared-projection energy law of the linear front-end (Theorem&nbsp;[-@thm-branch-weights]) and the Poisson-hazard race of the stochastic detector (Theorem&nbsp;[-@thm-born]) --- under explicit and disclosed assumptions to produce Born-distributed winners. Each layer is well-motivated physically (the squared projection by passive linearity and ideal extraction; the Poisson hazard by the candidate physical mechanism of Poissonian micro-absorption with rare-event thinning), but the combination *assumes* the structure rather than deriving it from anything more primitive. A fundamental derivation of the Born rule from sub-Born physics --- if such a thing is possible --- would have to come from a separate research program.

The construction does *not* prove Bell-nonlocal physics. The zero-sequence mode in our analog is a real classical common-mode signal carried on a physical wire; it is not a quantum entanglement channel in the strict sense. The structural analogy between the zero-sequence reservoir and AQFT edge modes (or the Bohmian quantum potential) is suggestive, but the analogy is not equivalent to a derivation. Whether the analogy reflects a deeper physical correspondence --- whether quantum entanglement is actually field-theoretic boundary energy of the kind our analog makes explicit --- is an open foundational question to which our work contributes a candidate finite-dimensional model but not a proof.

The construction does *not* provide a full detector theory. The shot-trigger nucleation hypothesis of Section&nbsp;[-@sec-born] is a functional specification: it states the hazard law $\lambda(P) \approx \alpha P$ that the detector must satisfy and demonstrates that detector families that meet this specification produce Born statistics, but it does not identify the underlying microscopic state variable that nucleates, the physical mechanism that makes the hazard linear (rather than exponential, saturating, or history-dependent), or the noise source that produces the stochasticity. These are open questions and are the subject of ongoing investigation.

The construction does *not* yet establish discrete one-shot outcomes from sub-detector physics. The Theorem&nbsp;[-@thm-born] derivation of Born statistics from a Poisson-hazard race is mathematically airtight, but it inserts the discreteness of the click event as a primitive (the first-event time of a Poisson process). It does not derive that primitive from a smoother underlying dynamics. Whether such a derivation is possible --- whether the discreteness of the click can emerge from a fundamentally smooth classical-field substrate, or whether it must be inserted as an axiom --- is again the kind of open question we localize but do not solve.

What the construction *does* establish, in the concrete and limited sense made precise throughout the paper, is that *a classical three-phase analog system computes the correct projective branch weights at the linear absorbed-energy level, that a shot-trigger detector race converts those weights into Born-distributed clicks under explicit assumptions, that a zero-sequence closure latch enforces single-shot exclusivity without contaminating the pre-click selection, and that the integrated chain reproduces Tsirelson-saturating CHSH within an explicit error budget*. This is a narrow but precise structural result, and we believe it is the most that can be claimed honestly about a finite-dimensional analog of this kind.

## Open questions

Five open questions are raised by the framework and not resolved in the present work. Each is a natural target for follow-up investigation.

*The microscopic origin of the linear hazard law.* The shot-trigger nucleation hypothesis requires $\lambda(P) \approx \alpha P + \lambda_\text{dark}$ over a usable rare-event regime. The candidate mechanism --- Poissonian micro-absorption with rare-event thinning --- is consistent with this requirement but not yet derived from a specific physical device. Identifying or building a detector cell whose measured trigger rate satisfies the linear hazard law over a calibrated power range is a concrete experimental program that would close one of the largest gaps in the framework.

*Timescale separation between selection and completion.* The post-click-only architecture of the closure latch (Section&nbsp;[-@sec-latch]) requires the latch's pre-click contamination to be small. Section&nbsp;[-@sec-latch] gave an explicit tolerance condition $|\varepsilon|\, \alpha/(\Gamma + \beta) \leq 2\delta$ for differential pre-click feedback, but the underlying physical question --- what timescale separation is required between nucleation latency, closure rise time, and winner drain time, in a real device --- remains open.

*The microscopic source of stochasticity.* The randomness in the present model is inserted at the detector hazard level. The underlying physical question --- whether the relevant randomness comes from thermal noise, shot noise, discrete absorption events, defect fluctuations, environmental jitter, or some combination --- has not been answered. Different sources predict different rate laws and different correlations, and identifying the right source is part of the same experimental program as identifying the linear-hazard mechanism.

*Branch-hazard independence under finite closure.* The Theorem&nbsp;[-@thm-born] derivation assumes the four branch hazards are conditionally independent given the common envelope $\gamma(t)$. If the branches are coupled through a residual common-mode channel even before closure (i.e., if the closure variable is not strictly zero pre-click), the independence assumption fails, and the Born statistics may distort. The pre-click backaction proposition of Section&nbsp;[-@sec-latch] gives the perturbative tolerance bounds; whether realistic implementations sit safely inside this bound is an empirical question.

*$D_4$ and higher symmetry-enhanced violations.* As noted under predictions, systems with $D_4$ symmetry possess additional independent quadratic invariants beyond the three of $C_3$. Whether these additional invariants produce violations of generalized Bell inequalities beyond those accessible to the three-phase system --- and whether they can be implemented in a similarly tractable lumped-element analog --- is the natural extension of the framework to richer symmetry classes.

## Implications for foundations

The interpretation of Bell violations developed in this paper has three foundational implications, stated cautiously.

*Nonlocality is not an irreducible feature of distant measurement.* On the present reading, the apparent nonlocality of CHSH violations is the signature of a global conservation constraint on a tripartite system, projected onto a two-party measurement subspace that omits the channel doing the conservation work. When the omitted channel is restored to the bookkeeping, the correlations become as natural as momentum conservation in a two-body decay --- nonlocal in the same trivial sense, but enriched by the algebraic factor of two that distinguishes amplitude conservation from intensity conservation. The strangeness of Bell violations is, on this reading, not the strangeness of action at a distance but the strangeness of incomplete accounting.

*The distinction between linear and quadratic conservation is foundational.* The hierarchy table of Section&nbsp;[-@sec-hierarchy] places the Bell--Tsirelson gap precisely in the algebraic gap between linear and quadratic conservation. Any program that aims to derive quantum mechanics from a deeper substrate --- whether a hidden-variable theory, a sub-quantum dynamics, or a thermal-statistical principle --- must explain the role of squaring: why the conserved quantity in the quantum case is intensity rather than amplitude, why the doubling identity $\cos^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 + \cos 2x)$ enters the structure at the conservation level, and why the system's symmetries include the rotation group whose representation theory produces the doubled-angle correlator. These are not parameters that can be tuned; they are algebraic constraints that any successful sub-quantum theory must respect. The present construction makes them explicit.

*The "observed" world has structurally identifiable layers.* The construction separates four functionally distinct layers --- shared joint state, local analyzer rotations, stochastic nucleation detector, common-mode closure latch --- each addressing a different sub-problem of the measurement chain (joint correlation, no-signaling, single-shot click, exclusivity). Foundational programs that conflate these layers (treating the entire measurement as a single black box, or attributing all of quantum strangeness to "collapse") lose the structural information that the layered analysis preserves. Where exactly the residual mystery sits --- in the Born rule, in the discreteness of the click, in the binarization of continuous distributions, in the source of stochasticity --- can be localized layer by layer. Our analog does not solve any of these residual mysteries, but it locates each of them precisely, which is a precondition for solving them.

\newpage

# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

We have argued that Bell-inequality violations are signatures of the algebraic order of the conservation law governing a correlated source, and that the apparent nonlocality of two-party CHSH violations is the consequence of an incomplete accounting of an intrinsically three-party conservation law. We have constructed a classical three-phase analog system --- a passive linear front-end of four delta-LC tanks with shared resonant core, a shot-trigger Born-rule detector, and a zero-sequence closure latch --- and demonstrated by SPICE simulation that the integrated chain reproduces Tsirelson-saturating CHSH ($S \approx 2.828$, error $0.043$; winner-law RMS error $0.013$; decisive rate $99.5\%$; energy conservation to numerical tolerance) under explicit and disclosed assumptions and a non-local conservation constraint mediated by the zero-sequence mode.

The five core findings, restated in their tightest form:

1. *The form of Bell-correlation functions is determined by the algebraic order of the source's conservation law.* Linear conservation ($\mathbf{p}_A + \mathbf{p}_B = 0$) produces correlations $E \propto \cos(\Delta\phi)$ with CHSH $|S| \leq \sqrt{2}$. Quadratic conservation ($V_\alpha^2 + V_\beta^2 + V_0^2 = \mathrm{const}$) produces correlations $E \propto \cos(2\Delta\phi)$ with CHSH $|S| \leq 2\sqrt{2}$. The factor of two between the two cases is the double-angle identity $\cos^2 x = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 + \cos 2x)$ promoted from arithmetic to physics.

2. *The CHSH violation arises from this algebraic doubling.* The progression from stochastic-local ($\sqrt{2}$) through deterministic threshold ($2$) to quantum quadratic ($2\sqrt{2}$) follows step-by-step factors of $\sqrt{2}$, with each step's mechanism (factorized coin flips, sign-thresholding, strict event-by-event complementarity) algebraically explicit. The Tsirelson bound is the maximum CHSH value achievable by binary projections of a single positive-definite quadratic form on a compact rotational symmetry group.

3. *The two-party CHSH framework is an incomplete accounting of a three-party conservation law.* The Clarke decomposition $V_\alpha^2 + V_\beta^2 + V_0^2 = \mathrm{const}$ has three modes; CHSH measures the first two and projects out the third. The zero-sequence mode $V_0$ absorbs the energy that the two analyzers fail to capture, with a $\theta$-dependent profile $P_0(\theta) = -\cos(\Delta\phi)\cos(2\theta - \phi_A - \phi_B)$ that vanishes at orthogonal analyzer settings, oscillates at full amplitude at aligned settings, and takes intermediate values precisely where CHSH violation peaks.

4. *The third party is structurally analogous to the AQFT vacuum / edge mode and the Bohmian quantum potential.* In the algebraic-quantum-field-theory picture of entanglement, the zero-sequence mode corresponds to the boundary modes shared between two regions; in Bohmian mechanics, it corresponds to the quantum potential's nonlocal coupling. In our analog these abstract structures are realized as a measurable common-mode signal on a physical wire. The three perspectives --- AQFT edge modes, Bohmian quantum potential, monogamy of entanglement budget --- are three views of the same algebraic fact: a quadratic conservation law on a bipartite system has an irreducibly tripartite accounting.

5. *A classical three-phase analog with a linear front-end, a shot-trigger detector, and a zero-sequence closure latch reproduces Tsirelson-saturating CHSH under disclosed assumptions and a non-local conservation constraint.* The SPICE realization in `physical_front_end_candidate/` achieves $S = 2.828 \pm 0.043$, winner-law RMS $0.013$, decisive rate $99.5\%$, and energy conservation to numerical tolerance. The chain does not refute Bell's theorem (the zero-sequence coupling is non-local); it makes the locus of nonlocality concrete and physically measurable, and demonstrates that the structure of quantum correlations is reproducible by a classical conservation-respecting analog.

The combined framework suggests that the foundations of quantum mechanics and the engineering of three-phase power systems share more than a superficial structural similarity. They are different representations of the same algebraic geometry: quadratic conservation laws on phase spaces with rotational symmetry, with the apparent nonlocality of one being the Clarke-decomposition zero-sequence mode of the other. If this identification holds up under the more detailed engagement with prequantum classical models that Section&nbsp;[-@sec-prior-art] sketched, it will have implications well beyond the specific construction presented here --- for the interpretation of entanglement entropy in quantum field theory, for the operational meaning of the quantum potential in Bohmian mechanics, and for the design of classical analog systems that mimic increasingly large fragments of quantum behavior under explicit and bounded conservation constraints.

What this paper has established is narrow but precise: a finite-dimensional, lab-buildable, SPICE-validated classical analog reproduces the Tsirelson-saturating cos-squared correlator, with the locus of its non-classicality identified explicitly as the zero-sequence energy reservoir and the limits of its scope disclosed at every layer of the construction. Whether the structural correspondence runs deeper --- whether quantum mechanics itself is, in some operationally defensible sense, the field-theoretic limit of a three-phase quadratic-conservation algebra --- is the question the framework opens but does not close. We leave it open with the hope that the analog presented here will be useful as a concrete reference point for thinking about it.

# Clarke Transform Conventions and Identities {#sec-appendix-clarke}

This appendix records the conventions of the Clarke and Park transforms used throughout the paper, proves the power-invariance identity that underlies the conservation hierarchy of Section&nbsp;[-@sec-hierarchy], and collects the algebraic identities used in the derivations.

## A.1 The amplitude-invariant and power-invariant Clarke transforms

Two conventions for the Clarke transform are in common use. The *amplitude-invariant* convention preserves peak voltage amplitudes through the transformation,
$$
T_\text{amp} \;=\; \frac{2}{3}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -\tfrac{1}{2} & -\tfrac{1}{2} \\ 0 & \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ \tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{2} \end{pmatrix},
$$
while the *power-invariant* convention preserves the sum of squares (instantaneous power),
$$
T_\text{pwr} \;=\; \sqrt{\tfrac{2}{3}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -\tfrac{1}{2} & -\tfrac{1}{2} \\ 0 & \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{pmatrix}.
$$
We use the power-invariant form throughout. It is the convention under which Parseval's identity holds without rescaling, which is the property the paper uses repeatedly.

## A.2 Power invariance (Parseval)

The defining property of the power-invariant Clarke transform is orthonormality, $T_\text{pwr}^T T_\text{pwr} = I_3$. Direct verification: the rows of $T_\text{pwr}$ have norm-squared $\tfrac{2}{3}(1 + \tfrac{1}{4} + \tfrac{1}{4}) = 1$, $\tfrac{2}{3}(\tfrac{3}{4} + \tfrac{3}{4}) = 1$, $\tfrac{2}{3}(\tfrac{3}{2}) = 1$, and pairwise dot products are zero. Therefore for any $(v_a, v_b, v_c)$ and the transformed $(v_\alpha, v_\beta, v_0) = T_\text{pwr}(v_a, v_b, v_c)^T$,
$$
v_\alpha^2 + v_\beta^2 + v_0^2 \;=\; (T_\text{pwr}\mathbf{v})^T(T_\text{pwr}\mathbf{v}) \;=\; \mathbf{v}^T T_\text{pwr}^T T_\text{pwr}\mathbf{v} \;=\; \mathbf{v}^T \mathbf{v} \;=\; v_a^2 + v_b^2 + v_c^2.
$$
This is the identity used as the conservation law in Section&nbsp;[-@sec-clarke] and as the foundation of the three-party accounting in Section&nbsp;[-@sec-third-party].

## A.3 Symmetrical components and the relation to Clarke

The symmetrical-component decomposition [@fortescue1918] uses the cube-root-of-unity rotation $a = e^{i 2\pi/3}$ and the matrix
$$
T_\text{sym} \;=\; \frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & a & a^2 \\ 1 & a^2 & a \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
A balanced three-phase signal is mapped into positive-, negative-, and zero-sequence components $(v_+, v_-, v_0)$. The Clarke and Fortescue representations are related by a unitary transformation on the $\alpha\beta$ plane: if $\hat{v} = v_\alpha + i v_\beta$ is the complex Clarke amplitude, then for purely-real inputs $v_\pm = \tfrac{1}{2}\hat{v}$ and the zero-sequence component is identical in the two decompositions.

## A.4 The Park rotation

The Park transform is a rotation of the Clarke $\alpha\beta$ plane by a tunable angle $\phi$:
$$
P(\phi) \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \cos\phi & \sin\phi \\ -\sin\phi & \cos\phi \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \begin{pmatrix} v_d \\ v_q \end{pmatrix} \;=\; P(\phi) \begin{pmatrix} v_\alpha \\ v_\beta \end{pmatrix}.
$$
$P(\phi)$ does not couple to the zero-sequence axis. For a positive-sequence input $v_\alpha = V\cos\theta$, $v_\beta = V\sin\theta$, the rotated components are $v_d = V\cos(\theta - \phi)$, $v_q = V\sin(\theta - \phi)$, and the $d$-axis power is the squared projection $V^2\cos^2(\theta - \phi)$, which is Malus's law.

## A.5 Identities used in derivations

The following identities are used in Sections&nbsp;[-@sec-hierarchy], [-@sec-two-party], and [-@sec-third-party]:

*Double-angle.* $\cos^2 x = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 + \cos 2x)$ and $\sin^2 x = \tfrac{1}{2}(1 - \cos 2x)$. Their sum is unity (the strict-complementarity identity).

*Product-to-sum.* $\cos x \cos y = \tfrac{1}{2}[\cos(x-y) + \cos(x+y)]$ and $\cos x \sin y = \tfrac{1}{2}[\sin(x+y) - \sin(x-y)]$. The first is used in deriving the linear correlator $E_\text{lin} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\cos(\Delta\phi)$ from the source integral, and the second in deriving the orthogonality of the negative-sequence component.

*Sum of two squared cosines.* $\cos^2 x + \cos^2 y = 1 + \cos(x-y)\cos(x+y)$. Used in Section&nbsp;[-@sec-third-party] to compute $P_A(\theta) + P_B(\theta) = 1 + \cos(\Delta\phi)\cos(2\theta - \phi_A - \phi_B)$, the central identity of the zero-sequence reservoir argument.

*Orthogonality on the circle.* $\int_0^{2\pi}\cos(m\theta + \alpha)\,\cos(n\theta + \beta)\,d\theta/(2\pi) = \tfrac{1}{2}\cos(\alpha - \beta)\,\delta_{mn}$ for $m, n \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$. Used to evaluate the integrals over the hidden phase $\theta$ in Sections&nbsp;[-@sec-hierarchy] and [-@sec-two-party].

# Reduced Four-Mode Model: Component-by-Component Derivation {#sec-appendix-reduced}

This appendix supplies the explicit derivation of the singlet branch weights $w_{xy}(a, b)$ from $\Psi(a, b) = (R_A(a) \otimes R_B(b))\, \Psi_\text{singlet}$, together with the resulting correlator. The result is stated without proof in Section&nbsp;[-@sec-reduced-model]; here we work it out term by term.

## B.1 Setup

The singlet-like state in the joint basis $\{|{++}\rangle, |{+-}\rangle, |{-+}\rangle, |{--}\rangle\}$ is
$$
\Psi_\text{singlet} \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
Local analyzers are real rotations
$$
R(\theta) \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix},
$$
so $R_A(a) \otimes R_B(b)$ is the $4\times 4$ Kronecker product. With $c_a = \cos a$, $s_a = \sin a$, $c_b = \cos b$, $s_b = \sin b$:
$$
R_A(a) \otimes R_B(b) \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} c_a c_b & c_a s_b & s_a c_b & s_a s_b \\ -c_a s_b & c_a c_b & -s_a s_b & s_a c_b \\ -s_a c_b & -s_a s_b & c_a c_b & c_a s_b \\ s_a s_b & -s_a c_b & -c_a s_b & c_a c_b \end{pmatrix}.
$$

## B.2 The rotated state

Apply $U(a, b) = R_A(a) \otimes R_B(b)$ to $\Psi_\text{singlet}$. Only the second and third basis components of $\Psi_\text{singlet}$ contribute:
$$
\Psi(a, b) \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \big( U_{:,2} \cdot 1 + U_{:,3} \cdot (-1) \big).
$$
Reading the columns of the Kronecker product:
$$
U_{:,2} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} c_a s_b \\ c_a c_b \\ -s_a s_b \\ -s_a c_b \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
U_{:,3} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} s_a c_b \\ -s_a s_b \\ c_a c_b \\ -c_a s_b \end{pmatrix}.
$$
Therefore
$$
\Psi(a, b) \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix} c_a s_b - s_a c_b \\ c_a c_b + s_a s_b \\ -s_a s_b - c_a c_b \\ -s_a c_b + c_a s_b \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix} -\sin(a-b) \\ \cos(a-b) \\ -\cos(a-b) \\ -\sin(a-b) \end{pmatrix},
$$
using $\sin(a-b) = s_a c_b - c_a s_b$ and $\cos(a-b) = c_a c_b + s_a s_b$. The rotated state is parametrized by a single variable, $\Delta = a - b$.

## B.3 The branch weights

Squaring each component and dividing by the $\tfrac{1}{2}$ from the normalization:
$$
w_{++}(a,b) = w_{--}(a,b) = \tfrac{1}{2}\sin^2(a-b),
$$
$$
w_{+-}(a,b) = w_{-+}(a,b) = \tfrac{1}{2}\cos^2(a-b).
$$
The "same-outcome" probability is $P_\text{same} = w_{++} + w_{--} = \sin^2(a-b)$ and the "different-outcome" probability is $P_\text{diff} = w_{+-} + w_{-+} = \cos^2(a-b)$, summing to unity by the Pythagorean identity.

## B.4 The correlator

With outcome coding $+ \mapsto +1$, $- \mapsto -1$, the correlator is
$$
E(a, b) \;=\; w_{++} - w_{+-} - w_{-+} + w_{--} \;=\; \sin^2(a-b) - \cos^2(a-b) \;=\; -\cos\bigl(2(a-b)\bigr).
$$
This is the full-amplitude doubled-angle correlator, yielding $|S| = 2\sqrt{2}$ at the CHSH-optimal angles.

# Detector Family Characterization {#sec-appendix-detectors}

This appendix records the four detector families characterized in `detector_search/`, their parameter spaces, and their performance against the Theorem&nbsp;[-@thm-born] target.

## C.1 The four families

*Shot-trigger.* Hazard $\lambda = \lambda_\text{dark} + (P_\text{abs}/\varepsilon_\text{event})\, p_\text{trig}$, with $\varepsilon_\text{event}$ the energy per microscopic absorption event, $p_\text{trig} \in [0, 1]$ the per-event trigger probability, and $\lambda_\text{dark}$ the dark-count rate. Implements the Poissonian-micro-absorption-with-rare-event-thinning hypothesis. Parameter ranges: $\varepsilon_\text{event} \in [0.2, 5.0]$ (log), $p_\text{trig} \in [0.05, 0.99]$, $\lambda_\text{dark} \in [10^{-4}, 5\times 10^{-2}]$ (log), dead time $\in [0, 0.1]$.

*Poisson-linear.* Direct parametrization $\lambda = \lambda_\text{dark} + \alpha P_\text{abs}$. Parameter ranges: $\alpha \in [0.1, 2.0]$, $\lambda_\text{dark} \in [10^{-4}, 5\times 10^{-2}]$ (log), dead time $\in [0, 0.1]$. Mathematically equivalent to shot-trigger in the regime where $\varepsilon_\text{event}$ and $p_\text{trig}$ enter only through their product; characterizing both serves as a robustness check.

*Accumulator (bad control).* Smooth-energy-accumulator-with-deterministic-threshold. The branch's accumulated energy follows $dE = P_\text{abs}\,dt + \sigma\, dB$, and a click is registered when $E$ first crosses $L$. Included as an explicit negative control.

*Metastable-escape.* Kramers-style escape over an energy barrier of height $V_b$ tilted by absorbed power: $\lambda = \lambda_0 \exp(-V_b/(k_BT)) \cdot \exp(\beta P_\text{abs})$. Approximately linear only in the weak-tilt regime $\beta P_\text{abs} \ll 1$.

## C.2 Search and ranking

Empirical ranking from `artifacts/detector_search/`:

| Family                      | Race-law fidelity (RMS) | Comment                                                |
|-----------------------------|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| Shot-trigger                | $\sim 10^{-3}$          | Best; Theorem&nbsp;[-@thm-born] applies cleanly        |
| Poisson-linear              | $\sim 10^{-3}$          | Equivalent to shot-trigger in linear regime            |
| Metastable-escape           | $\sim 10^{-2}$          | Approx.\ Born in weak-tilt; degrades with stronger $\beta P_\text{abs}$ |
| Accumulator (bad control)   | $\sim 10^{-1}$          | Fails Born; concentrates on max-weight branch          |

The shot-trigger family is selected as the working detector model for the SPICE chain. Parameters used in the integrated chain: $\varepsilon_\text{event} \approx 1.25$, $p_\text{trig} \approx 0.9$, $\lambda_\text{dark} \approx 0.02$, dead time $\approx 0$.

# SPICE Component Values for the Preferred Chain {#sec-appendix-spice}

This appendix records the explicit component values used in the SPICE realization of Section&nbsp;[-@sec-spice], drawn from `physical_front_end_candidate/preferred_front_end_netlist_candidate.py`. The values are reported in normalized units; conversion to physical $\mathrm{H}$, $\mathrm{F}$, and $\Omega$ is done by choosing a reference impedance and frequency, and is left for hardware fabrication.

## D.1 Architectural summary

The SPICE chain is a passive linear network with the following structure: (i) a balanced four-port preparation drive feeding (ii) four delta-LC tank modules indexed by the joint basis $\{++, +-, -+, --\}$; (iii) an antisymmetric coupling between the $|{+-}\rangle$ and $|{-+}\rangle$ tanks; (iv) per-branch analyzer couplers implementing the local rotations $R_A(a) \otimes R_B(b)$; and (v) per-branch resistive readout terminations.

## D.2 Component values

The reference configuration is "implementation option C" of `PreferredFrontEndNetlistConfig`, with the following values (units are dimensionless / normalized):

| Component group         | Symbol               | Value (or four-tuple) | Notes                                          |
|-------------------------|----------------------|-----------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| Source angular freq     | $\omega_0$            | $1.0$                  | Common tank frequency in normalized units      |
| Singlet coupling        | $\kappa$              | $0.27$                 | Antisymmetric coupling between $|{+-}\rangle$, $|{-+}\rangle$ tanks |
| Tank linewidth          | $\gamma$              | $0.008$                | Common damping per tank                        |
| Tank inductance         | $L_t$                 | $1.0$                  | Identical across all four tanks                |
| Tank capacitance        | $C_t$                 | $1.0$                  | Tuned to $\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{L_t C_t}$         |
| Source resistance       | $R_s$ (per branch)    | $(25.0, 25.2, 24.9, 25.1)$ | $\sim 0.4\%$ parametric tolerance         |
| Source inductance       | $L_s$ (per branch)    | $(0.18, 0.184, 0.176, 0.182)$ | Driver-side coupling inductance       |
| Load resistance         | $R_L$ (per branch)    | $(50.0, 49.9, 50.1, 49.8)$ | Termination at the readout                |
| Readout shunt cap.      | $C_\text{sh}$         | $(0.06, 0.058, 0.061, 0.059)$ | Tank-side shunt to ground             |
| Internal loss res.      | $R_\text{int}$        | $(16.67, 16.54, 16.79, 16.62)$ | Tank-internal dissipation            |
| Bridge resistance       | $R_b$                 | $10.0$                 | Antisymmetric-coupling bridge element          |
| Bridge capacitance      | $C_b$                 | $0.42$                 | Bridge-element shunt                           |
| Side coupling cap.      | $C_\text{side}$       | $0.035$                | Lateral coupling between adjacent tanks         |
| Return coupling cap.    | $C_\text{return}$     | $0.014$                | Common-mode return path                        |
| Hybrid drive mix        | $\mu_h$               | $0.12$                 | Preparation-drive mode-mix coefficient         |
| Branch gain trim        | $g_\text{br}$         | $(1.0, 0.999, 1.001, 0.9985)$ | Per-branch gain offsets ($< 0.15\%$)    |
| Branch phase trim       | $\delta\phi_\text{br}$ | $(0.0, 0.6, -0.4, 0.8)^\circ$ | Per-branch phase offsets ($< 1^\circ$)  |

: Component values for the preferred SPICE chain (normalized units). {#tbl-spice-bom}

## D.3 Inductance matrix structure

The $11 \times 11$ self/mutual-inductance matrix has block structure: (a) a diagonal block for the four tanks at $L_t$ with per-branch trims; (b) a source-coupling block for the four source-side coils; (c) the antisymmetric coupling between tank 2 and tank 3 (the $|{+-}\rangle$ and $|{-+}\rangle$ tanks): $M_{23} = -\kappa\sqrt{L_t L_t} = -\kappa L_t$, sign carried by winding orientation, placing the singlet $|\psi_s\rangle$ as an eigenmode with eigenvalue $\omega_0 + 2\kappa$; (d) side and return couplings via $C_\text{side}$ and $C_\text{return}$. The full matrix is built by `physical_front_end_candidate/preferred_front_end_netlist_candidate.py` and checked for positive-definiteness on every solve.

## D.4 Analyzer coupler parameterization

Alice's coupler at angle $a$ has $\alpha$- and $\beta$-axis coupling coefficients
$$
k_{A,\alpha} = k_A\,(1 + \varepsilon_A)\cos a, \qquad k_{A,\beta} = k_A\,(1 - \varepsilon_A)\sin a,
$$
where $k_A$ is the nominal coupling and $\varepsilon_A$ is the analyzer-asymmetry parameter that the phase-descent calibration of [@nobles2026phase] is designed to detect. For the symmetric configuration, $\varepsilon_A \approx 0$ to within construction tolerance ($\sim 0.4\%$). Bob's coupler is parametrized identically with angle $b$.

# Full Numerical Results {#sec-appendix-results}

This appendix records the full numerical results of the SPICE realization, broken out per analyzer-pair setting, for the headline CHSH evaluation.

## E.1 Per-pair branch weights and correlators

The CHSH test sweeps four analyzer-pair configurations: $(a, b) \in \{(0, \pi/8), (0, 3\pi/8), (\pi/4, \pi/8), (\pi/4, 3\pi/8)\}$. For each pair, the SPICE chain produces four branch energies $\hat{E}_{xy}$, normalized to four empirical weights $\hat{w}_{xy}$, against analytic Born targets $w_{xy}^\text{th} = \tfrac{1}{2}\sin^2(a-b)$ for $\{++, --\}$ and $\tfrac{1}{2}\cos^2(a-b)$ for $\{+-, -+\}$.

| Setting $(a, b)$ | $\Delta\phi$ | $w_{++}^\text{th}$ | $w_{+-}^\text{th}$ | $\hat{w}_{++}$ | $\hat{w}_{+-}$ | RMS err | $\hat{E}(a,b)$ | Target $E^\text{th}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $(0, \pi/8)$       | $-\pi/8$    | $0.0732$ | $0.4268$ | $0.075$ | $0.428$ | $0.013$ | $-0.704$ | $-\sqrt{2}/2$ |
| $(0, 3\pi/8)$      | $-3\pi/8$   | $0.4268$ | $0.0732$ | $0.421$ | $0.078$ | $0.012$ | $+0.708$ | $+\sqrt{2}/2$ |
| $(\pi/4, \pi/8)$   | $+\pi/8$    | $0.0732$ | $0.4268$ | $0.071$ | $0.430$ | $0.011$ | $-0.713$ | $-\sqrt{2}/2$ |
| $(\pi/4, 3\pi/8)$  | $-\pi/8$    | $0.0732$ | $0.4268$ | $0.077$ | $0.426$ | $0.014$ | $-0.703$ | $-\sqrt{2}/2$ |

: Per-pair branch weights and correlators from the SPICE chain. Aggregate winner-law RMS = $0.013$; aggregate CHSH magnitude $|S| \approx 2.828$ vs. $2\sqrt{2} \approx 2.8284$. {#tbl-spice-results}

## E.2 Robustness sweep summary

A robustness analysis perturbs each component value over $\pm 2\%$ tolerance and re-evaluates the chain.

| Perturbation               | Component group     | $\Delta$(winner-law RMS) | $\Delta|S|$ |
|----------------------------|---------------------|--------------------------|-------------|
| $\pm 1\%$ on $\kappa$       | Singlet coupling    | $+0.005$                  | $-0.018$     |
| $\pm 2\%$ on $L_t, C_t$     | Tank LC             | $+0.010$                  | $-0.030$     |
| $\pm 2\%$ on $R_L$          | Load resistance     | $+0.003$                  | $-0.008$     |
| $\pm 2\%$ on $g_\text{br}$  | Branch gain trim    | $+0.012$                  | $-0.038$     |

: Robustness of the SPICE chain to component-value perturbations. From `make spice-driven-robustness-report`. {#tbl-spice-robustness}

The chain is most sensitive to $\kappa$ (singlet-coupling parameter) and to per-branch gain trim, and most robust to load-resistance perturbations.

## E.3 Latch performance

The closure latch metrics from the integrated chain at $4{,}000$ trials per angle pair:

- *Decisive rate:* $99.5 \pm 0.2\%$. Timeouts ($\sim 0.5\%$) concentrated at angle pairs with extreme branch-weight asymmetry.
- *Winner-drain dominance:* $99.97\%$ of post-click absorbed energy through the winning branch.
- *Energy conservation:* $< 10^{-9}$ relative error on every trial.
- *Pre-click contamination:* zero by construction; $Z(t) = 0$ identically until the first nucleation.
